explanation: A dead-equal rook endgame -- Re7, Rh4, Rxe3, and several other rook moves are all exactly 0.00 here. Nothing to calculate, just don't do anything careless.
Nh3+ forces gxh3, the only way to deal with the check, then Qg2 is mate -- the king has nowhere left to go. A classic knight-sac-to-clear-the-mating-square pattern.
You're already a bit better here and c3, c4, or Nc4 all keep a similar edge by solidifying the center before pushing further. Not a single key move -- just don't loosen your position for no reason.
Qe7 keeps the full advantage (+455), eyeing ...Bc5 next. In the real game this position is drawn from, Qc7 was played instead, giving back a big chunk of the edge (+196) for no real reason.
Roughly balanced queen endgame -- Qf3+, Rf8, and Kh8 are all within 15 points of each other. Trading checks or just repositioning, it doesn't matter much which here.

Qa5+ keeps real pressure (forking the king and threatening ...Qxe5+ next). In the real game this is drawn from, e6 was played instead, ignoring the bishop hanging on g4 -- White's Nxg4 won it outright. Worth flagging the move that LOOKS best here and isn't: Bxd1 grabs the queen for a bishop, but it allows Bf7# -- immediate mate. Your king on e8 has no escape once that lands: d7 and f7 are both covered by the knight on e5, and e7, f8, d8 are all blocked by your own pawn, bishop, and queen. Qa5+ wins specifically because it's check, which takes that whole idea off the table for White.

Your d-pawn is two squares from queening with real threats behind it (+256). In the real game, Rb8 was played instead, which doesn't address that at all -- the chance to press it evaporated, and the position dropped to roughly equal instead of a clear advantage.

Ng4+ forks the king and the bishop on e3 in one move -- check first, then the bishop's gone next. Rxf6+ looks tempting too but it's dramatically weaker (+2 instead of +252) since it gives up the fork for a much smaller gain.

fxg4 just wins the piece sitting there (+329). In the real game, Rd1+ was played instead -- a check, but it doesn't grab any material, and the follow-up (Kg2, then White's Rxe7) handed back most of the advantage for the privilege of checking first.
A pawn's hanging on b4 and several ways to deal with it work about equally well -- Nxb4, Bxb4, and Rb8 all land within 20 points of each other.

f3 pushes your passed pawn with the game essentially decided (+1194, close to a forced win). In the real game, Rgg2 was played instead -- still winning (+664) but giving back real ground by not pressing the pawn. The game was won by checkmate anyway, but the cleaner path was sitting right there.
Kg1 stops the g-pawn from ever promoting. In the real game, Rb1 was played instead, and g1=Q+ just promoted right through it, giving back almost the entire advantage for one move of carelessness.

Already in real trouble here -- even Qf3, the best try available, leaves you worse (-508). In the real game, Rd1 was played instead, giving up more ground still (-768), though there wasn't a clean save on the table either way.

White has to deal with Black's d-pawn, one square from queening with threats. gxf4+ removes the attacking knight with check and defuses it; anything passive here (Kg1, f3) walks straight into a forced mate.

White's a7 and b7 pawns are both one step from queening and your king can't stop both at once -- this position was already lost regardless of what gets played here. In the real game, Kc7 was played, which just speeds up the inevitable; even the best try barely changes the outcome.
King safety shuffle in a roughly balanced position -- Ke2 is marginally best but Ke1 holds just as well. Small stuff, not a tactic.

Rg8+ is the rook on g2 moving with check -- which also clears the diagonal for your bishop on f1, so Bxh3 captures Black's queen next move. The check and the discovered line-opening happen in the same move, which is the whole point of the combination.

Bxc5 trades into a forced sequence (Nxc5 Qxe5 Re8 Qxc5) that nets real material by the end -- not one flashy shot, just the only line here that doesn't hand the initiative to Black's queen on a8 instead.

A white knight is hanging on e7 -- Nxe7 and Qxe7 both just win it back, interchangeably (within 20 points of each other). Not finding the capture at all is the actual mistake, which is why Kh8 drops nearly 200 points by comparison.
Another dead-drawn minor-piece endgame -- Ke5, Ke6, and h6 are all 0.00. Staying calm and not forcing anything is the whole skill being tested.
